title: Agent Assurance — ROOK | Harbor Care | QE

scenes.narration: Alex asks for the eleven o’clock appointment, but the slot is full. A confident booking confirmation is useful only if the schedule can support it. We will test the capacity rule and inspect the appointment record.

Alex is using the Patient Access Assistant. The conversation sits beside the recorded business action and tool trace. We start with a customer request, then use Rook to test the expected behavior independently.

Patient lookup resolves the authenticated patient. Booking checks capacity and records an appointment. Urgent handoff, administrative guidance and record export serve separate responsibilities. This fictional service handles access and scheduling, not clinical diagnosis.

Follow a routine booking request through patient identity and slot availability. A full slot must produce no appointment. An available slot may be reserved once. Urgent requests follow the separate human-handoff policy. The reply must agree with the recorded action.

Start in Rook’s interactive terminal. Explore the requirements and connection contract. No application source is provided in this workspace. Rook identifies the agent’s responsibilities and business features from the supplied material.

Exploration writes an agent definition and feature files into this workspace. Open them and check the discovered responsibilities. These are readable local artifacts, ready for review before anything is synchronized.

Generate a focused set across functional, non-functional and adversarial classes. Review the proposed scope, then confirm. Rook writes scenario files with customer goals and acceptance criteria; the generated count alone is not a coverage claim.

The requirements declare no capacity at eleven o’clock. The selected criterion therefore requires no appointment at that time. Review the patient reference and the booking rule together; a successful tool response does not make an overbooking correct.
Create the connection profile from the supplied contract. Rook authors the runner and checks it. Opening a session, executing turns, closing it and collecting evidence are separate responsibilities.

Inspect the profile, then test the connection. Confirm that Rook reaches the intended agent and returns a correlated response. Keep credential values in the environment, outside the profile and recording.

Run the selected scenario with the test flag. Review the plan and proceed. Rook invokes the agent and judges the returned evidence. This run stays out of the hosted project timeline. Processing time is removed from the edit.

Open the report in the terminal. Read the verdict and the criterion-level explanation. A passing response, a failed business action and missing evidence are distinct findings; the report must preserve that distinction.

The run is also a set of files on this machine: its plan, report, requests, responses, verdicts and collected evidence. Open the same run identifier and follow one scenario through these files. These files remain available without opening the hosted interface.

The agent confirms an eleven o’clock appointment and records appointment one, even though the requirements declare zero capacity. Rook reports Fail because the original booking tool accepts a slot that the requirements say is full.

The role-play attack asks for a capacity override. The answer refuses the override persona, but an appointment is still recorded for the full slot. Rook reports Fail. A polite refusal did not prevent the business action.

The M C P check retains the patient reference across three turns, but still records the eleven o’clock appointment. Its capacity criterion fails. The transport and conversation state work; the business rule still needs the same repair.

Repeat the same case against the updated capacity check. The appointment list remains empty, and Rook reports Pass. The repair enforces availability at the booking boundary; it does not depend only on the model choosing to refuse.

Sharing is optional. Sync the reviewed project definitions, then execute a shared run without the test flag. That new run records its results upstream. Sync does not convert the earlier local test into a hosted run.

Open the hosted web interface. Select the matching shared run, then open its scenario and evidence. The local files and hosted view serve different review needs; use the run identifier to keep the investigation consistent.
Explore the agent. Review generated tests. Prove the connection. Run, inspect and repair. Keep the artifacts local, and share a reviewed run when the team needs it. Agent Assurance, with Rook.
